title: STOMATIN-DEFICIENT CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS WITH NEUROLOGIC DEFECTS
alt_titles: GLUT1 DEFICIENCY SYNDROME WITH PSEUDOHYPERKALEMIA AND HEMOLYSIS
CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS, STOMATIN-DEFICIENT, WITH MENTAL RETARDATION, SEIZURES, CATARACTS, AND MASSIVE HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene (138140) on chromosome 1p34.2.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC) is a rare form of stomatocytosis. Its features include a cold-induced cation leak from red cells, hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, together with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation and movement disorder (Fricke et al., 2004; Flatt et al., 2011). Flatt et al. (2011) showed that the disorder results from mutations in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT1, and described it as a novel form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome. In this disorder the red cell membrane is abnormally permeable to sodium and potassium, which can cause pseudohyperkalemia (Bawazir et al., 2012).

checks.evidence_quote: These patients are the only two known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis.
checks.explanation: The paper presents it as a variant of hereditary stomatocytosis with only two known cases, so 'rare' follows directly.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) reported 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree with stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis, and gave further details on 1 previously reported case. Two of these patients had stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, and the authors stated that they were the only 2 known cases of this variant. Both had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Fricke et al. (2004) suggested that this probably defined a new hemato-neurologic syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) reported an infant with GLUT1 deficiency and a cation-leaky red cell state. The infant presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly. Seizures developed later, and developmental milestones were delayed. MRI and CT scans of the brain showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. Vision was impaired by both cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The authors stated that this was the fourth pedigree described with this syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) studied erythrocyte membrane proteins in 2 patients with congenital hemolytic anemia caused by increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K. One patient had hereditary stomatocytosis and the other had cryohydrocytosis. On 1-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis, the band 7 proteins separated into components of approximately 30,000, 28,000 and 26,000 daltons, and the 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients. Two-dimensional electrophoresis separated the normal 28,000-dalton component into 2 proteins, designated 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, whereas 60 x 8 was present as usual. All band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were invariably present in normal subjects and in reticulocytosis controls.

paragraphs.text: In all of their cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis, Fricke et al. (2004) found by Western blotting of red cell membranes that the 32-kD membrane protein stomatin was deficient. All cases had pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete. On typical blood films, some red cells were stomatin-positive and most were negative, although in 1 case only a minority were negative. All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin-positive. The cases differed markedly in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. Three cases showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. The other 2 showed a minimum at about 20 to 25 degrees C, so that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, giving the cryohydrocytosis phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In an infant with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene that results in deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436 of GLUT1. The infant had erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly, and later developed seizures and delayed development. Vision was impaired by cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The red cells were extremely leaky to cations and lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way, which explained the patient's pseudohyperkalemia.
